title: Julien veut partir  (Julien Wants to Leave)

segments.t: In the lounge of the laser game center, Gabriel spots musician and filmmaker Julien Dore looking anxious to leave. After Julien admits to a creative dispute, Gabriel pushes actress Sofia Leprince to seize the moment and introduce herself. Listen to the scene in French first. Don't worry about catching every word.
Tu peux me trouver un taxi?
Je me suis disputé avec Charlotte.
Elle ne comprend pas la fin.
Now let's break down the scene step by step. Listen to each line, followed by its meaning and a short explanation.
'Hi Julien! Are you doing well?' Asking 'you go well?' is the standard friendly check-in among friends in French, using 'go' instead of 'do'.
Tu peux me trouver un taxi?
'Can you find me a taxi?' Slipping 'for me' right ahead of 'to find' needs no 'for' in French—just a single two-letter object marker.
'Is there a problem?' Keeping 'there is a problem' unchanged and lifting your pitch at the end is the fastest spoken way to ask if something is wrong in French.
Je me suis disputé avec Charlotte.
'I argued with Charlotte.' Adding 'myself' turns 'disputed' into an everyday reflexive expression meaning 'had a quarrel' or 'argued' in French.
Elle ne comprend pas la fin.
'She does not understand the ending.' Related to English 'comprehend', this core everyday action is the normal way to say 'understand' in French.
'I must go back to Paris.' Built on 're-enter', the action after 'must' means 'go home' or 'head back' in French.
'Sofia wants to do screen tests.' Literally 'tries'—and the source of English 'essay'—the final word means 'auditions' or 'screen tests' in cinema French.
'We will see about that later.' Irregular future 'will see' needs no 'about' before 'that' in French, ending with 'more late' to mean 'later'.
'You are too pushy, Gabriel!' Literally 'too heavy', calling someone 'heavy' in casual slang means they are being 'clumsy', 'annoying', or 'pushy' in French.
'He is not interested.' Notice the double 's' inside the cognate 'interested', keeping a crisp 's' sound between vowels in French.
'Stop worrying like that.' Unlike English '-ing', 'stop' links to 'worry yourself' with 'of' in French, closing with 'like that'.
'Julien is always very stressed.' Putting 'always' right after 'is' matches English placement here, paired with the familiar cognate 'stressed'.
'You must give it a shot.' Literally 'tempt the blow', this punchy three-word idiom is what you'd say to urge a friend to 'take a chance' or 'give it a shot'.

'All right, I will talk to him.' Placing 'to him' ahead of 'to speak' needs no separate 'to' word in French—that three-letter marker covers 'to him' or 'to her'. Now let's listen to the whole exchange once more from beginning to end.
Tu peux me trouver un taxi?
Je me suis disputé avec Charlotte.
Elle ne comprend pas la fin.

Despite her initial hesitation, Sofia gathers her courage to approach Julien Dore. Notice how French uses a lively idiom about trying a blow when encouraging someone to take a chance. See you next time!

source.show: Dix pour cent (Call My Agent!) S02E03

lines.fragment: Tu peux me trouver un taxi ?
Charlotte et moi on s'est disputés à propos du film.
Dis-moi si tu veux organiser des essais voix avec Sofia.
Il n'est visiblement pas intéressé par moi.
Ah, c'est super que tu sois venu.
